title: Colorado Child's Flu Death, the Season's First, Renews Vaccination Push
excerpt: The elementary-aged child had no record of a flu shot. Last season killed eight Colorado children, and barely one in ten residents is vaccinated as this season starts early.
body:
• Colorado has confirmed its first pediatric flu death of the 2026–27 respiratory season: an elementary-aged child from outside the Denver metro area, with no record of receiving this season's flu vaccine.
  • Last season was Colorado's deadliest for children in more than two decades outside the 2009 H1N1 pandemic — eight pediatric flu deaths, five of them in unvaccinated children.
  • Vaccination coverage is lagging: only about 8% of Colorado children aged 6 months to 9 years and 5% of those 10–19 had a flu shot so far this season; statewide coverage is 9.5%, a point below last season.
  • Flu shots are free or low-cost at Colorado pharmacies and clinics; 58 people are currently hospitalised with flu in the state, the most since April.

Colorado's respiratory virus season has recorded its first child death from influenza. The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment said the elementary-aged child, from outside the Denver metro area, died this week, and that there is no record the child received this season's flu vaccine, Colorado Public Radio reported.

"The flu is not a cold. The flu can be deadly in individuals that are otherwise healthy."

— Dr. Michelle Barron, infectious diseases physician, UCHealth

A season starting early, after a record year

The death follows Colorado's worst pediatric flu season in more than 20 years outside a pandemic: eight children died last season. Five were unvaccinated, four had no vaccination record in the state database, and one was younger than six months — too young to be vaccinated at all. Only the 2009–10 H1N1 pandemic season was worse, with 12 confirmed pediatric deaths. This season, flu is circulating earlier than usual while case numbers are still relatively low, and 58 Coloradans are hospitalised with flu, the most since the end of April.

The vaccination gap

State immunisation data, tracked on the health department's respiratory virus dashboard, show how thin coverage is heading into the holidays. About 8% of children from six months to nine years and 5% of 10- to 19-year-olds have had a flu shot; even the most vaccinated group, those 65 and older, is only at about 21%. Statewide coverage of 9.5% runs about a percentage point below last season, and rates among Hispanic Coloradans are the lowest at around 3%.

Dr. Barron's warning is aimed at the assumption that healthy children do not need the shot. Parents may think a child without asthma or other conditions does not need flu immunisation, she said — "they do." With Thanksgiving travel weeks away and flu, COVID-19 and RSV all circulating, health officials say now is the ideal window to vaccinate against all three; shots are available free or at low cost at pharmacies, clinics and doctors' offices across the state. For Indian American families — among the groups that gather multigenerationally through the Diwali and holiday season — the practical step is the same one officials repeat every year, this time backed by a death in October rather than January: vaccinate the children before the gatherings start.
